name: Act of April 29, 1874 ratifying the Brunot Agreement with the Ute Indians
citation: Act of April 29, 1874, ch. 136, 18 Stat. 36 (Kappler, vol. 1, p. 151)
nations: Southern Ute Indian Tribe (Muache and Capote bands)
Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation (Tabeguache or Uncompahgre, Yampa, Grand River and Uintah bands)
promises: Article I: the Confederated Bands gave up a block of their 1868 reservation in the San Juan Mountains, except any part of Uncompahgre Park found to lie south of the new line, which stayed in the reservation.
Article II: the United States would let the Utes hunt on the ceded land so long as the game lasts and the Indians are at peace with the white people.
Article III: the United States would set apart, as a perpetual trust for the Utes, money or bonds enough to yield $25,000 a year, for their use annually forever.
Article IV: an agency for the Weeminuche, Muache and Capote bands would be built in the southern part of the reservation when the President thought it necessary.

Article V: the 1868 treaty stayed in force, including its promise that no unauthorized persons would ever be permitted to pass over, settle on or reside in the reservation, except for the ceded country.
Sections 2 and 3 of the Act: the Treasury would hold five per cent bonds paying $25,000 a year in trust for the Utes, and pay Ouray $1,000 a year while he remained chief.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission held that the $507,662.84 paid for the cession of Royce area 566, land it valued at $8,500,000 as of April 29, 1874, was so grossly inadequate as to make the consideration unconscionable, and found the Confederated Bands entitled to the difference, subject to offsets.

landTaken: Royce area 566: about 3.7 million acres of the east-central portion of the reservation (402 U.S. 159). The Commission took April 29, 1874, the date of this Act, as the date of valuation.
compensation: The 1874 Act set up a fund of five per cent bonds paying $25,000 a year and paid Ouray $1,000 (18 Stat. 36, secs. 2 and 3). The Commission credited the United States with $507,662.84 as the price actually paid. After a stipulated compromise of offsets, the Commission entered final judgment for the Confederated Bands of Ute Indians for $7,908,586.16 on February 18, 1965 (Docket 327).
today: The Brunot Area is no longer reservation land. The Southern Ute Indian Tribe says the hunting right reserved in Article II remains, and that a 2008 agreement with Colorado lets its members hunt and fish there again under tribal rules.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says the 1873 Brunot Agreement ceded about 3.7 million acres of the San Juan Mountains, a major loss to the reservation and to its hunting way of life, but that the hunting right reserved in it remains undiminished; since a 2008 agreement with Colorado its members can once again hunt and fish there.

openQuestions: This entry and cession-1873-09-13-uta are the same cession (Royce area 566): the agreement and the Act that ratified it.
The Commission's 1962 opinion and findings, as scanned, date the agreement September 18, 1873; the agreement's own text and Royce say September 13, 1873, which is used here.

The Commission found the area of Royce area 566, less Uncompahgre Park (about 10,240 acres), to be 3,765,535 acres as the scan reads; the Supreme Court says 3.7 million acres. The exact figure was not cross-checked against a clean copy.
Whether and when the 1965 judgment was paid was not checked.
No Ute Mountain Ute or Ute Indian Tribe account of the Brunot cession was found; utemountainutetribe.com and utetribe.com had no history page that loaded on 2026-11-08.

Audit 2026-11-08: Docket 327 date checked. The 1962 opinion is internally inconsistent: it says September 18, 1873 in its statement of facts and September 13, 1873, the date the Brunot Agreement was signed, later on; the findings say September 18. The agreement text (Kappler vol. 1, p. 151) says the thirteenth, so September 13 stands. Figures ,662.84, ,500,000 and ,908,586.16 and the 1971 quote confirmed.

plain.promised: Congress approved the Ute bands giving up about 3.7 million acres of the San Juan Mountains, with a hunting right kept and a trust fund paying $25,000 a year forever.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission held the $507,662.84 paid for land worth $8,500,000 was unconscionable. The United States admitted in the Supreme Court that the payment was not made promptly.
plain.today: The Confederated Bands of Ute Indians won a final judgment of $7,908,586.16 in 1965. The Southern Ute Indian Tribe says its hunting right in the area remains.
